LTF-Course-Architecture.title: LTF-Course-Architecture
LTF-Course-Architecture.content:
French Reading Textbook
The French Reading Textbook is the language precision layer of Proustian.
It is not a generic French course. It is a reading course built toward Proust.
French is the target language. English is the scaffold language. Chinese is not the main scaffold for this track.
The first planning horizon is A0 to B1, roughly 50-60 chapters, at about one chapter per week.
Pedagogical Reliability
This is a targeted reading curriculum, not AI-generated improvisation.
It combines:

reading-knowledge French textbook tradition
classical-language reading textbook rigor
evidence-informed instructed SLA principles
input processing and form-meaning mapping
Anki repetition
self-tested diagnostic revision
Proust-specific target pressure

Ordinary French textbooks serve general language ability. This textbook serves reading competence toward Proust. It may skip conversation, travel situations, and general communicative tasks, but it must not skip reading grammar, vocabulary recognition, function words, reference, tense, subordination, or long-sentence parsing.

LTF-Proust-Target-Policy.title: LTF-Proust-Target-Policy
LTF-Proust-Target-Policy.content:
Proust Target Policy
The final target is Marcel Proust, À la recherche du temps perdu, in French.
The first book is not yet direct Proust reading. Early chapters prepare the reader for Proust by building structural sight.
Use Proust-oriented vocabulary when it helps:

memory
time
rooms
sensation
perception
signs
sentence movement
narration

Do not force fake Proustian depth into A0 lessons.
Model sentences may be controlled or adapted. They must be clearly marked as training sentences when they are not quotations.
Long Proust quotations should wait until the reader has enough grammar to parse them.

Vocabulary should support reading grammar and Proustian preparation.
Progression:

Cognates

Principles

Use high-yield reading vocabulary before topic vocabulary.
Teach function words early and repeatedly.
Mark false friends clearly.
Use Proust-oriented vocabulary without forcing fake Proustian depth into A0 lessons.
Keep vocabulary tied to sentence reading, not isolated memorization.
Treat vocabulary as a repeatable recognition system, not a list.
Convert vocabulary into cards only when each card tests one retrievable point.
Use failed cards to revise vocabulary presentation.

Acquisition Loop
cognate recognition → false friend warning → word family → function word → Proust lexical field → sentence encounter → Anki card → failed-card diagnosis → re-encounter

A0 to B1 Course Outline
The French Reading Textbook is the language precision layer of Proustian.
French is not an independent general course here. The goal is accelerated reading toward Proust by ignoring irrelevant general French topics while preserving essential reading grammar.
Plan first: A0 to B1, roughly 50-60 chapters.
Pace: about one chapter per week.
Sequence Rationale
The opening sequence follows reading-knowledge French textbook tradition:

cognates and visual recognition
false friends and controlled guessing
word families and recognition patterns
function words and relation marking
sentence structure

This sequence trains reading actions before interpretation. It also supports U1’s method: recognition first, claim second, textual return always.
Stage 0 — A0 — Seeing French
Goal: see the French sentence before interpretation.
Core work:

sentence boundaries
subject and verb
nouns, gender, and number
articles
basic word order
English structural control

Prototype chapters:

Recognizing French on the Page: Cognates and Reading Confidence
When English Misleads: False Friends and Controlled Guessing
Word Families: Suffixes, Prefixes, and Recognition Patterns

Stage 1 — A1 — Reading Skeleton
Goal: read simple French sentence skeletons.
Core work:

être and avoir
regular present tense
adjectives and agreement
prepositions
negation
basic objects and complements

Stage 2 — A2 — Narrative Memory Grammar
Goal: read basic narrative and memory structures.
Core work:

Stage 3 — B1 — Proustian Entry
Goal: enter controlled Proustian reading.

Language-Training/LTF-Chapter-001-Cognat.title: Chapter 001 — Cognates and Reading Confidence
Language-Training/LTF-Chapter-001-Cognat.content:
Chapter 001 — Cognates and Reading Confidence
Before You Begin
You do not need to know French grammar before starting this chapter. You need one reading habit: look at the French page before deciding that it is unreadable.
French and English share many learned words. Some come from Latin, some passed through French into English, and some belong to modern intellectual vocabulary. That shared material gives an English reader a first foothold.
The rule for this chapter is strict:
A familiar-looking word gives you a foothold. It does not give you the whole sentence.
A foothold is useful because it lets you stay on the page. It is dangerous only when you treat it as proof.
What You Will Learn
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

notice French words that resemble English words;
group common visual patterns such as -tion, -ité, -ment, -able, and -ible;
use accents and final -e as recognition clues without overtrusting them;
separate recognition from mastery;
mark footholds in a short training passage without trying to translate everything.

Core Reading Move
Use resemblance as a foothold, not as proof.
The reading action is:

Notice the resemblance.
Say only a simple support word.
Keep uncertainty open.
Continue through the phrase or sentence.

You are not trying to produce a polished translation. You are learning to remain calm when the page begins to look partly legible.
1. Explanation
A cognate is a word that resembles a word in another language because the two words share a history or because one language borrowed from the other. For reading, the history matters less than the action: the shape of the word gives you an initial support.
Look at these words:




























































FrenchFirst English supportProustian fieldmémoirememorymemorysensationsensationsensationimpressionimpressionperceptionattentionattentionattentionperceptionperceptionperceptionimageimageimagevisiblevisibleseeinginvisibleinvisibleseeingsilencesilenceatmospheremomentmomenttime
These are useful. But they are not complete. mémoire can mean memory as faculty, a memory, or a record. impression can be sensory, mental, or artistic. visible can describe something physically seen or something made intelligible.
Recognition tells you: “I have a handle.” Mastery tells you: “I know what this word is doing here.” In Chapter 001, you are training recognition, not pretending to have mastery.
Common recognition patterns













































PatternFrench examplesReading value-tionsensation, perception, attention, composition, transformationOften matches English -tion nouns.-itévérité, réalité, possibilité, sensibilité, obscuritéOften points toward English -ity nouns.-mentmoment, mouvement, sentiment, changement, jugementOften points toward English -ment, but check context.-ableadmirable, probable, capable, stable, comparableOften points toward English -able.-iblevisible, invisible, possible, sensible, perceptibleOften points toward English -ible; some are risky.final -eforme, image, nature, silence, phraseOften makes the word look French while still recognizable.accent cluesmémoire, réalité, vérité, émotion, écritureAccents change pronunciation and spelling; they may still preserve a recognizable shape.
Do not make a rule stronger than it is. Pattern recognition is a start. The sentence still decides.
2. Recognition
Read the following list as a recognition field. Do not memorize all of it today. Mark the words that give you a foothold.

This is more than forty examples. You do not need to own them. You need to see that the page is not blank.
3. Controlled Training
Exercise Set 1 — Find the foothold

perception

  Show answer
Possible support words: 1 memory; 2 sensation; 3 perception; 4 attention; 5 composition; 6 transformation; 7 reality; 8 possibility; 9 movement; 10 visible.
These are support words, not final translations.

Exercise Set 2 — Name the pattern
Choose the visible pattern: -tion, -ité, -ment, -able, -ible, final -e, or accent clue.

vérité
mouvement
admirable

émotion

  Show answer

Exercise Set 3 — Recognition is not mastery
Mark each item as safe foothold or needs context. Many correct answers are “needs context.”

mémoire = memory
impression = impression
visible = visible
nature = nature
sentiment = sentiment / feeling
indicible = unsayable
matière = matter / material
phrase = phrase / sentence


  Show answer
All eight are useful footholds. Items 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, and 8 especially need context. Even high-confidence words can change force inside a sentence. phrase, for example, usually means sentence in French, not only a musical or rhetorical phrase.

Exercise Set 4 — Group by field
Group the words into memory, sensation, seeing, abstraction, or art/form.

mémoire
sensation
image
vérité
composition
impression
visible
transformation
réalité
forme


  Show answer
Memory: mémoire. Sensation: sensation, impression. Seeing: image, visible. Abstraction: vérité, réalité. Art/form: composition, transformation, forme.
Other groupings can be defensible if you can explain the reading reason. The point is to form a reading field, not a perfect taxonomy.

4. Pattern Work
PATTERN-Cognate-Resemblance
Pattern
A French word resembles an English word closely enough to give an initial support.
Reading Move
Use the resemblance to stay on the page, then keep reading.
What It Usually Does
It gives a first semantic foothold: sensation, perception, visible, possible.
Do Not
Do not treat resemblance as proof of exact meaning.
Mini Example
une sensation visible → sensation + visible are footholds. The phrase still needs structure.
Where It Returns
Every chapter, especially false friends, word families, and passage cards.
PATTERN-Suffix-tion
Pattern
French -tion often matches English -tion nouns.
Reading Move
Recognize an abstract or action noun quickly.
What It Usually Does
It names a process, result, or abstraction: transformation, perception, attention.
Do Not
Do not assume the noun functions the same way in every sentence.
Mini Example
la transformation de la sensation → transformation is a process noun.
Where It Returns
Theory syntax, Deleuze vocabulary, and Proustian analysis.
PATTERN-Suffix-ite
Pattern
French -ité often corresponds to English -ity.
Reading Move
Recognize an abstract quality.
What It Usually Does
It turns a quality into a noun: réalité, possibilité, sensibilité.
Do Not
Do not flatten all -ité words into vague abstraction. Ask what quality is being named.
Mini Example
la possibilité d'une image → possibility is the named condition.
Where It Returns
Abstract prose, theory reading, and Proustian reflection on perception.
PATTERN-Suffix-ment
Pattern
French -ment can mark nouns such as mouvement, changement, jugement, and also later many adverbs.
Reading Move
Recognize the ending, then check the word type.
What It Usually Does
In this chapter it often gives a noun foothold: movement, change, judgment.
Do Not
Do not assume every -ment word is the same type. Later, lentement is an adverb.
Mini Example
un mouvement de mémoire → movement is a noun foothold.
Where It Returns
Word-family work and sentence skeletons.
5. Mini Reading
Gear 1 reading means the training surface is mostly English with selected French anchors. Read for footholds only.
A reader begins with mémoire, not because memory is simple, but because the word gives a first handle. A sensation appears before explanation. An impression becomes visible for a moment. The page is still difficult, but it is not empty. The reader can mark attention, perception, image, and transformation as footholds, then wait for the sentence to decide more.
Your task is not to translate the paragraph. Your task is to list the French anchors that help you stay with it.
6. Reading Notes
This course uses Proustian fields early: memory, sensation, impression, attention, image, time, and form. That does not mean you are already reading Proust. It means the first vocabulary you learn should point toward the future pressure of Proustian reading.
A general French course might begin with travel, food, or classroom phrases. This course begins with words that help you approach literary and theoretical pages.
7. Practice
Review Task — Mark only what you know
In the mini reading, list ten French anchors. Beside each one write:

high confidence if the English support is clear;
context needed if the word is familiar but flexible.

Practice Set — Foothold, not proof
For each phrase, underline the cognate foothold and write one uncertainty.

une impression visible
la mémoire sensible
une transformation possible
la réalité de l'image
un mouvement de perception
une composition admirable
la forme invisible
une émotion obscure
la possibilité d'un silence
une attention comparable


  Show answer
Possible footholds: impression / visible; mémoire / sensible; transformation / possible; réalité / image; mouvement / perception; composition / admirable; forme / invisible; émotion / obscure; possibilité / silence; attention / comparable.
Possible uncertainties: exact relation between words, whether an adjective is literal or abstract, whether the phrase names a physical, mental, or artistic state.

Check Your Answer
You are succeeding if you can point to a familiar-looking French word without claiming too much. You should be able to say: “This word gives me a support, but I still need the phrase or sentence.”
What You Can Now Do
You can open a French page and find footholds. You can recognize common learned-word patterns. You can resist the two beginner errors: panic and overconfidence.
Next Chapter
Next you will learn why some familiar-looking words mislead you.

Language-Training/LTF-Chapter-002-False-.content:
Chapter 002 — False Friends and Controlled Guessing
Before You Begin
Chapter 001 trained resemblance as a foothold. This chapter adds discipline. Some words look familiar and still mislead you.
The point is not to distrust French. The point is to slow down your first English reflex.
French-English resemblance is a clue, not proof.
What You Will Learn
You will learn to:

distinguish a false friend from a partial cognate;
use the sequence Recognize → suspend → verify → reread;
check a guess against the sentence;
avoid mechanical English substitutions;
read a short passage where familiar-looking words create traps.

Core Reading Move
Recognize → suspend → verify → reread.
That means:

Recognize the familiar shape.
Suspend the automatic English guess.
Verify with context, word type, and phrase pattern.
Reread the sentence with the safer meaning.

1. Explanation
A false friend is a word that looks like an English word but usually means something different.
A partial cognate is a word that can share an English meaning in some contexts but has other common meanings too.
Compare:



































FrenchBad automatic guessSafer readingactuellementactuallycurrently / at presentattendreattendto wait forlibrairielibrarybookstorebibliothèquebibliographylibrarydéceptiondeceptiondisappointment
The problem is not the first guess. The problem is stopping there.
For Proustian reading, this matters because first impressions are powerful. A sensation, an image, or a remembered scene can seem clear before it has been understood. Your reading habit should match that discipline: notice the first impression, then test it.
2. Recognition
Study the table as a warning map. Do not memorize it mechanically. Use it to train hesitation.

4. Pattern Work
PATTERN-False-Friend-Alert
Pattern
A French word looks like an English word but usually means something different.
Reading Move
Pause the automatic English guess and verify.
What It Usually Does
It protects you from confident misreading: actuellement, attendre, librairie, déception.
Do Not
Do not punish yourself for the first guess. Correct it by rereading.
Mini Example
Le lecteur attend. → The reader waits, not “attends.”
Where It Returns
Every time resemblance feels too easy.
PATTERN-Partial-Cognate
Pattern
A French word overlaps with English in some contexts but not all.
Reading Move
Keep two or more possible readings open until the sentence narrows them.
What It Usually Does
It prevents over-fixed translation: expérience, figure, caractère, histoire.
Do Not
Do not memorize only one English equivalent.
Mini Example
une expérience étrange may be a strange experience or a strange experiment.
Where It Returns
Theory prose and literary description, where abstract nouns shift force.
PATTERN-Controlled-Guessing
Pattern
A first guess is useful only when it can be tested.
Reading Move
Recognize → suspend → verify → reread.
What It Usually Does
It turns uncertainty into a method instead of panic.
Do Not
Do not leave the first guess untested.
Mini Example
la lecture looks like lecture, but the phrase around it may demand reading.
Where It Returns
All later sentence and passage work.
5. Mini Reading
Read slowly. This passage deliberately contains false friends and partial cognates.
Actuellement, le lecteur attend dans une librairie. Il ne cherche pas une bibliothèque. Il demande un livre sur la mémoire. Dans le coin, une figure reste visible sur la couverture. Cette image provoque une déception légère, puis une envie de lecture. L'expérience est sensible, mais son caractère reste obscur.
First pass: underline familiar-looking words.
Second pass: mark the dangerous ones.
Third pass: write a cautious reading in plain English.
6. Reading Notes
This mini reading is not Proust. It is a training surface for future Proustian reading. The fields are relevant: memory, image, reading, disappointment, desire, perceptible experience, obscure character. Those fields return often in literary and theoretical prose.
The important action is not vocabulary collection. The action is controlled rereading.
7. Practice
Exercise Set 4 — Verify by context
For each phrase, explain what makes the bad guess fail.

dans une librairie
il demande un livre

  Show answer
1 librairie is a bookstore; books are bought there. 2 demander takes the sense ask for. 3 attendre means wait. 4 sensible means perceptible or sensitive. 5 journée is a day span. 6 location is rental. 7 prévenir means warn or notify. 8 envie is desire, not envy here. 9 habit is clothing. 10 délai is a period / time limit; context decides whether delay is acceptable.

Review Task — Reread the mini reading
Write five dangerous words from the mini reading. For each one, write:

first bad guess;
safer reading;
context clue.

Check Your Answer
You are succeeding if you can slow down without freezing. A false friend should make you more accurate, not more afraid of French.
What You Can Now Do
You can use resemblance with judgment. You can identify high-risk familiar words, hold a guess lightly, and reread after correction.
Next Chapter
Next you will learn how to build families of related words so that one known form helps you read several new forms.

Chapter 003 — Word Families and Recognition Patterns
Before You Begin
Chapter 001 gave you footholds. Chapter 002 taught you to test them. Chapter 003 adds a new move: when you meet an unfamiliar word, look for its family before opening the dictionary.
A word family lets you read more than you have memorized.
A family does not guarantee meaning. It gives you a field of possible meaning.
What You Will Learn
You will learn to:

recognize related French forms;
use suffixes and prefixes as reading clues;
notice noun, adjective, and adverb tendencies;
build a small family before choosing a dictionary meaning;
read abstract vocabulary without treating every word as isolated.

Core Reading Move
Build a family before opening the dictionary.
The action is:

Notice the base or shared shape.
Gather nearby family forms.
Guess the word type.
Make a cautious reading.
Verify in the sentence.

1. Explanation
A word family is a group of related forms. The forms may not mean the same thing, but they help each other become visible.
Compare:





























FamilyReading fieldmémoire / mémorable / mémorisermemory, memorable, to memorizesentir / sensation / sensible / sensibilitésensing, sensation, perceptible, sensitivityvoir / visible / vision / invisibleseeing, visible, vision, invisibleécrire / écriture / écrivain / inscriptionwriting, script, writer, inscriptionlire / lecture / lisible / illisiblereading, readable, unreadable
You do not need full verb conjugations yet. You need to recognize that forms belong together.
A0 reading is often a matter of reducing loneliness. A word is less lonely when you can place it inside a family.
2. Recognition
Study these families. Read across, not down.




























































Base fieldFamily examplesWord-type tendencymemorymémoire, mémorable, mémoriser, mémorisationnoun / adjective / verb / nounsensationsentir, sensation, sensible, sensibilité, sentimentverb / noun / adjective / noun / nounseeingvoir, visible, vision, invisible, visibilitéverb / adjective / noun / adjective / nounwritingécrire, écriture, écrivain, inscription, réécrireverb / noun / noun / noun / verbreadinglire, lecture, lisible, illisible, lecteurverb / noun / adjective / adjective / nountransformationtransformer, transformation, transformable, transformateurverb / noun / adjective / nounperceptionpercevoir, perception, perceptible, imperceptibleverb / noun / adjective / adjectiveimaginationimaginer, imagination, imaginable, imageverb / noun / adjective / nouncompositioncomposer, composition, compositeur, composéverb / noun / noun / adjectivedistinctiondistinguer, distinction, distinct, indistinctverb / noun / adjective / adjective
More examples for pattern recognition:













































PatternExamplesReading cluere-revoir, relire, revenir, reprendreagain / backin- / im-invisible, impossible, imperceptible, immobilenot / un- / in--tionperception, transformation, distinction, mémorisationprocess / result noun-itésensibilité, visibilité, possibilité, intensitéabstract quality noun-able / -iblemémorable, transformable, lisible, perceptibleable to be / capable of being-eur / -ainlecteur, compositeur, écrivainperson or agent tendency-mentmouvement, changement, lentement, clairementnoun or adverb; check type
3. Controlled Training
Exercise Set 1 — Build the family
For each base word, list two related forms from the chapter.

mémoire
sentir
voir
écrire
lire
transformer
percevoir
imaginer
composer
distinguer


  Show answer
Possible answers: mémoire → mémorable, mémoriser; sentir → sensation, sensible; voir → visible, vision; écrire → écriture, écrivain; lire → lecture, lisible; transformer → transformation, transformable; percevoir → perception, perceptible; imaginer → imagination, imaginable; composer → composition, compositeur; distinguer → distinction, distinct.

Exercise Set 2 — Guess the word type
Mark noun, adjective, verb, or unknown / check context.

sensation
visible
lire
écriture
perceptible
transformation
mémorable
clairement
lecteur
impossible


  Show answer
1 noun; 2 adjective; 3 verb; 4 noun; 5 adjective; 6 noun; 7 adjective; 8 adverb; 9 noun/person; 10 adjective.
This is recognition, not full grammar. Context can still change function.

Exercise Set 3 — Prefix reading
Write the likely prefix value.

invisible
impossible
imperceptible
relire
revoir
réécrire
reprendre
indistinct


  Show answer
1 not visible; 2 not possible; 3 not perceptible; 4 read again; 5 see again; 6 write again; 7 take again / resume; 8 not distinct.

4. Pattern Work
PATTERN-Word-Family-Expansion
Pattern
One known form helps you recognize related forms.
Reading Move
Build a small family before isolating the word.
What It Usually Does
It turns an unknown word into a related word: lecture connects to lire; visible connects to voir.
Do Not
Do not assume every family member has the same meaning or force.
Mini Example
une image invisible → visible / invisible belongs to the seeing family.
Where It Returns
Vocabulary banks, Pattern Cards, and Passage Cards.
PATTERN-Suffix-Recognition
Pattern
A suffix gives a clue about word type and meaning field.
Reading Move
Use -tion, -ité, -able, -ible, and -ment as first sorting tools.
What It Usually Does
It helps identify abstract nouns, adjectives, and some adverbs.
Do Not
Do not treat suffixes as mechanical translation rules.
Mini Example
la visibilité d'une image → -ité marks an abstract quality noun.
Where It Returns
Theory syntax and long abstract sentences.
PATTERN-Noun-Adjective-Adverb-Guess
Pattern
Form clues can suggest whether a word names a thing, describes a thing, or modifies an action.
Reading Move
Make a cautious word-type guess before interpreting.
What It Usually Does
It keeps the sentence organized.
Do Not
Do not replace grammar with guessing. Use the guess to keep reading, then verify.
Mini Example
une sensation perceptible → sensation likely names; perceptible likely describes.
Where It Returns
Chapter 005 sentence skeletons.
5. Mini Reading
La mémoire rend une sensation mémorable. Une image visible devient parfois invisible. L'écriture transforme une impression en inscription. La lecture rend le mouvement de la pensée plus lisible, mais une perception obscure reste parfois imperceptible.
First pass: underline family links.
Second pass: mark nouns and adjectives.
Third pass: write one cautious sentence about what the passage is doing.
6. Reading Notes
This chapter prepares a future reader for abstract prose. Proustian and theoretical writing often builds with families: memory and memorable, perception and perceptible, reading and legibility, image and visibility.
The goal is not etymology. The goal is reading momentum.
7. Practice
Exercise Set 4 — Family map
Create a three-column map: noun, adjective, verb. Fill what you can.

mémoire / mémorable / mémoriser
sensation / sensible / sentir
vision / visible / voir
écriture / lisible? / écrire
lecture / lisible / lire
transformation / transformable / transformer


  Show answer
1 noun mémoire, adjective mémorable, verb mémoriser. 2 noun sensation, adjective sensible, verb sentir. 3 noun vision, adjective visible, verb voir. 4 noun écriture, no exact adjective from the set, verb écrire. 5 noun lecture, adjective lisible, verb lire. 6 noun transformation, adjective transformable, verb transformer.

Exercise Set 5 — Read by family, not dictionary first
For each phrase, identify the family and give a cautious reading.

une sensation sensible
une image invisible
une écriture lisible
une transformation perceptible
un souvenir mémorable
une distinction obscure
une composition visible
un mouvement imperceptible
une lecture difficile
une inscription claire


  Show answer
1 sensing family: a perceptible/sensitive sensation. 2 seeing family: an invisible image. 3 writing/reading family: readable writing. 4 transformation/perception family: a perceptible transformation. 5 memory family: a memorable recollection. 6 distinction family: an obscure distinction. 7 composition/seeing family: visible composition. 8 movement/perception family: an imperceptible movement. 9 reading family: difficult reading. 10 writing family: clear inscription.

Review Task — Before the dictionary
Choose five unfamiliar words from this chapter. For each one, write:

family;
likely word type;
cautious support meaning;
what the sentence must still verify.

Check Your Answer
A good answer does not need perfect translation. It should show that you can connect forms and avoid treating every word as isolated.
What You Can Now Do
You can read beyond memorized vocabulary. You can build a family, guess word type, and verify meaning in the sentence.
Next Chapter
Next you will shift from word families to the small relation words that connect phrases.

Chapter 004 — Function Words I
Before You Begin
The first three chapters trained you to notice large recognizable words. This chapter turns to small words.
Small words are easy to skip because they look thin. But in French reading, they often tell you how the sentence is built.
Small words build relations.
What You Will Learn
You will learn to:

recognize nine high-frequency function words;
ask what each small word connects;
avoid automatic translations such as “de = of” and “à = to”;
read relation before interpretation;
compress short phrases into relation notes.

Core Reading Move
Small words build relations.
The action is:

Circle the function word.
Identify what it connects.
Name the relation.
Delay polished translation.

1. Explanation
Function words do not usually carry the biggest dictionary meaning. They organize relations.























































WordRelation fieldDo not translate automatically asdesource / possession / relation / materialonly “of”àdirection / destination / relation / useonly “to”etadditiondecorative “and”maiscontrasta pause without forcedansinside / withinalways physical “in”suron / about / overonly physical “on”avecwith / accompanied byvague togethernesssanswithoutabsence as an afterthoughtcommeas / likeonly comparison, never role
The basic question is not “What is the English word?” The basic question is “What relation does this create?”
2. Recognition
de
de can mark source, possession, relation, or material.

la mémoire de l'enfance → relation / possession: memory of childhood
une impression de silence → relation / quality: an impression of silence
une table de bois → material: a wooden table
sortir de la chambre → source: come out of the room

Do not read every de as a flat “of.”
à
à can mark direction, destination, relation, or use.

aller à la chambre → direction / destination
un livre à lire → use / task: a book to read
une attention à l'image → relation / target
donner à la mémoire → direction toward a receiver

Do not read every à as a flat “to.”
et / mais
et adds. mais contrasts.

la mémoire et l'image → addition
la mémoire revient, mais l'image reste obscure → contrast

dans / sur
dans places something inside a frame. sur places something on, about, or over a surface or topic.

dans la chambre → inside a room
dans la mémoire → within memory
sur la table → on the table
sur la mémoire → about memory

avec / sans
avec marks accompaniment. sans marks absence.

avec une sensation → with a sensation
sans image → without an image

comme
comme can mean as or like. It creates comparison or role.

comme une image → like an image
comme lecteur → as a reader

3. Controlled Training
Exercise Set 1 — Identify the function word
Circle the function word and name it.

dans la chambre
une impression de silence
avec une sensation
sans image
la mémoire et le temps
la mémoire revient, mais l'image change
sur la table
un livre à lire
comme une vision
sortir de la chambre


  Show answer
1 dans; 2 de; 3 avec; 4 sans; 5 et; 6 mais; 7 sur; 8 à; 9 comme; 10 de.

Exercise Set 2 — Name the relation
Choose source, possession/relation, material, direction, addition, contrast, inside, about/on, accompaniment, absence, or comparison/role.

la mémoire de l'enfance
aller à la fenêtre
dans la mémoire
sur la mémoire
avec attention
sans souvenir
comme une sensation
le temps et l'habitude
obscur, mais visible
une table de bois


  Show answer
1 possession/relation; 2 direction; 3 inside/within; 4 about/on; 5 accompaniment or manner; 6 absence; 7 comparison; 8 addition; 9 contrast; 10 material.

Exercise Set 3 — Avoid mechanical translation
Replace the bad mechanical reading with a relation note.

une impression de silence → not just “of”; relation: ____
un livre à lire → not just “to”; relation: ____
dans la pensée → relation: ____
sur le temps → relation: ____
comme lecteur → relation: ____
sans attention → relation: ____


  Show answer
1 quality/relation; 2 use/task; 3 within a mental frame; 4 about a topic; 5 role; 6 absence.

4. Pattern Work
PATTERN-de
Pattern
de marks source, possession, relation, or material.
Reading Move
Ask what two elements are being linked and what kind of relation holds them.
What It Usually Does
It attaches one noun or phrase to another.
Do Not
Do not translate it automatically as “of.”
Mini Example
une impression de silence → an impression related to silence.
Where It Returns
Every chapter after this one, especially Proustian noun groups.
PATTERN-a
Pattern
à marks direction, destination, relation, or use.
Reading Move
Ask whether something points toward a place, task, receiver, or target.
What It Usually Does
It creates orientation.
Do Not
Do not translate it automatically as “to.”
Mini Example
un livre à lire → a book for reading / to be read.
Where It Returns
Infinitive phrases, reading tasks, and later sentence attachments.
PATTERN-dans
Pattern
dans places something inside or within a frame.
Reading Move
Find the frame.
What It Usually Does
It can frame physical space or mental space.
Do Not
Do not assume the frame is always physical.
Mini Example
dans la mémoire → within memory.
Where It Returns
Proustian rooms, memory spaces, and mental frames.
PATTERN-avec
Pattern
avec marks accompaniment.
Reading Move
Ask what is present together with the main action or thing.
What It Usually Does
It adds an accompanying element: person, tool, quality, or manner.
Do Not
Do not ignore it as a small optional word.
Mini Example
avec attention → with attention / attentively.
Where It Returns
Descriptions of reading, perception, and attention.
5. Mini Reading
Dans la chambre, le lecteur regarde une image avec attention. La mémoire de l'enfance revient, mais elle revient sans clarté. Sur la table, un livre sur le temps reste ouvert, comme une invitation à lire.
First pass: circle every function word.
Second pass: write what each one connects.
Third pass: compress the relations before translating.
6. Reading Notes
Proustian reading depends on relations: memory of childhood, sensation in a room, attention to an image, a book about time, a perception without clarity. If you skip the small words, you keep the vocabulary but lose the structure.
This chapter does not teach every use of de or à. It teaches a reading habit: relation first.
7. Practice
Exercise Set 4 — What does it connect?
For each phrase, write the two connected elements.

la mémoire de l'enfance
une sensation dans la chambre
une image sur la table
un regard avec attention
une impression sans forme
la lecture et la mémoire
un livre sur Proust
comme une image
une invitation à lire
obscur mais visible


  Show answer
1 mémoire + enfance; 2 sensation + chambre; 3 image + table; 4 regard + attention; 5 impression + absence of form; 6 lecture + mémoire; 7 livre + Proust as topic; 8 comparison to image; 9 invitation + reading task; 10 two contrasting qualities.

Exercise Set 5 — Compress before translating
Write a relation note, not a full translation.

dans la chambre
sur la mémoire
avec une sensation obscure
sans image visible
comme un souvenir
à la fenêtre
de la matière
et le silence
mais la perception change
un livre à relire


  Show answer
1 inside room frame; 2 about memory; 3 accompanied by an obscure sensation; 4 absence of visible image; 5 comparison to a memory; 6 direction/destination toward the window; 7 source/material/relation depending sentence; 8 addition of silence; 9 contrast with changing perception; 10 book for rereading.

Review Task — Relation map
From the mini reading, list five function words. For each, write:

function word;
what it connects;
relation created;
one bad mechanical translation to avoid.

Check Your Answer
You are succeeding if you can explain the relation before translating. A small word is not a decoration. It is a hinge.
What You Can Now Do
You can slow down at de, à, dans, sur, avec, sans, comme, et, and mais. You can ask what they connect and what relation they build.
Next Chapter
Next you will use word recognition and relation words to find the skeleton of a French sentence.

Chapter 005 — What Is a French Sentence?
Before You Begin
You can now recognize footholds, distrust false confidence, build word families, and read small relation words. Chapter 005 gives those skills a sentence frame.
A French sentence is not a cloud of words. It has a skeleton.
A long Proustian sentence is not magic. It is a sentence with many attachments.
In this chapter you will not learn full French syntax. You will learn the first reading action for any French sentence: find the subject, find the conjugated verb, and delay interpretation.
What You Will Learn
You will learn to identify:

subject;
conjugated verb;
complement;
modifier;
noun group;
opening frame;
adjective;
prepositional phrase;
word order;
sentence before interpretation.

Core Reading Move
Find the subject. Find the conjugated verb. Delay interpretation.
The action is:

Ignore the urge to translate immediately.
Find the subject group.
Find the conjugated verb.
Mark the complement if there is one.
Treat the rest as attachments until you can place them.

1. Explanation
The minimal skeleton for now is:
Subject + conjugated verb + complement
Not every sentence has a complement, but this pattern is the first stable model.
Step 1
La mémoire transforme une sensation.

























PartFrenchReading roleSubjectLa mémoirewhat the sentence starts fromConjugated verbtransformethe main actionComplementune sensationwhat is transformed
Step 2
La mémoire transforme une sensation obscure en image.
The skeleton is still:

Subject: La mémoire
Conjugated verb: transforme
Complement: une sensation obscure
Attachment / result phrase: en image

Step 3
Dans la chambre, la mémoire transforme une sensation obscure en image.
Now there is an opening frame:

Opening frame: Dans la chambre
Subject: la mémoire
Conjugated verb: transforme
Complement: une sensation obscure
Attachment / result phrase: en image

The sentence became longer, but the skeleton did not disappear.
2. Recognition
Terms for this chapter









































TermWorking meaningsubjectthe noun group the verb is built aroundconjugated verbthe verb form carrying the sentence action or statecomplementa word or group that completes the verb or phrasemodifiera word or group that adds description, place, time, or mannernoun groupa noun with its article and possible adjectiveopening framea phrase before the core sentence, often place or timeadjectivea describing word attached to a nounprepositional phrasea relation phrase beginning with a word such as dans, de, à, avec, sans, sur
Progressive examples



























































SentenceSubjectVerbComplement / attachmentLe souvenir revient.Le souvenirrevientnoneUne image apparaît.Une imageapparaîtnoneLa mémoire transforme une sensation.La mémoiretransformeune sensationLe lecteur observe une image.Le lecteurobserveune imageDans la chambre, une sensation revient.une sensationrevientopening frame: dans la chambreLa sensation obscure devient visible.La sensation obscuredevientvisibleLe silence transforme la perception.Le silencetransformela perceptionAvec attention, le lecteur relit la phrase.le lecteurrelitla phrase; opening frame: avec attention
Do not interpret first. Place the pieces first.
3. Controlled Training
Exercise Set 1 — Find subject and verb
For each sentence, write the subject and conjugated verb.

Le souvenir revient.
Une image apparaît.
La mémoire transforme une sensation.
Le lecteur observe une image.
La chambre reste silencieuse.
Une impression devient visible.
Le temps change la perception.
La lecture commence.
Le silence accompagne l'image.
Une sensation obscure revient.


  Show answer
1 subject Le souvenir, verb revient. 2 Une image, apparaît. 3 La mémoire, transforme. 4 Le lecteur, observe. 5 La chambre, reste. 6 Une impression, devient. 7 Le temps, change. 8 La lecture, commence. 9 Le silence, accompagne. 10 Une sensation obscure, revient.

Exercise Set 2 — Mark the complement
Write the complement if there is one. If there is no complement, write none.

La mémoire transforme une sensation.
Le lecteur relit la phrase.
Une image apparaît.
Le silence accompagne l'image.
La sensation devient visible.
Le temps change la chambre.
Une impression reste obscure.
Le narrateur observe la table.
La lumière transforme l'image.
Le souvenir revient.


  Show answer
1 une sensation; 2 la phrase; 3 none; 4 l’image; 5 visible as complement of state; 6 la chambre; 7 obscure as complement of state; 8 la table; 9 l’image; 10 none.

Exercise Set 3 — Separate opening frame from core
Mark the opening frame, then give the core sentence.

Dans la chambre, la mémoire transforme une sensation.
Avec attention, le lecteur relit la phrase.
Sur la table, une image reste visible.
Sans bruit, le souvenir revient.
Dans la mémoire, une impression change.
Comme une image, la sensation revient.


  Show answer
1 frame Dans la chambre; core la mémoire transforme une sensation. 2 frame Avec attention; core le lecteur relit la phrase. 3 frame Sur la table; core une image reste visible. 4 frame Sans bruit; core le souvenir revient. 5 frame Dans la mémoire; core une impression change. 6 frame Comme une image; core la sensation revient.

4. Pattern Work
PATTERN-Sentence-Skeleton
Pattern
A sentence has a recoverable skeleton even when it looks long.
Reading Move
Find subject + conjugated verb + complement before interpreting.
What It Usually Does
It prevents long sentences from becoming a blur.
Do Not
Do not translate from left to right before finding the verb.
Mini Example
Dans la chambre, la mémoire transforme une sensation obscure en image. → core: memory transforms a sensation.
Where It Returns
Every Proustian passage and every later syntax chapter.
PATTERN-Subject-Conjugated-Verb
Pattern
The subject and conjugated verb form the first anchor of the sentence.
Reading Move
Locate the noun group and the finite verb.
What It Usually Does
It tells you what the sentence is doing before you chase details.
Do Not
Do not mistake every nearby noun for the subject.
Mini Example
Le silence accompagne l'image. → subject Le silence; verb accompagne.
Where It Returns
All reading skeleton work.
PATTERN-Attachments-Light
Pattern
Extra phrases attach to the skeleton as frames, descriptions, or relation phrases.
Reading Move
Mark attachments lightly without overanalyzing them.
What It Usually Does
It lets you keep the sentence open without drowning in detail.
Do Not
Do not introduce full relative clauses yet. That comes later.
Mini Example
Avec attention, le lecteur relit la phrase dans la chambre. → frame/manner + core + place attachment.
Where It Returns
Longer sentences, Passage Cards, and future Proustian syntax.
5. Mini Reading
Dans la chambre, la mémoire transforme une sensation obscure en image. Le lecteur observe cette image avec attention. Sur la table, un livre reste ouvert. Le silence accompagne la lecture, mais une impression change la perception du moment.
First pass: find each conjugated verb.
Second pass: find each subject.
Third pass: mark opening frames and attachments.
6. Reading Notes
This is the first bridge from vocabulary to sentence. Proustian sentences can become long because they gather frames, noun groups, adjectives, and prepositional phrases. You are not ready to parse all of that yet. You are ready to keep returning to the skeleton.
A long sentence becomes less frightening when you can say: “Here is the core. These other pieces attach to it.”
7. Practice
Exercise Set 4 — Compress the sentence
Reduce each sentence to a skeleton note.

Dans la chambre, la mémoire transforme une sensation obscure en image.
Avec attention, le lecteur relit la phrase difficile.
Sur la table, une image ancienne reste visible.
Sans explication, le souvenir revient dans la mémoire.
La perception du moment change la lecture.
Une sensation presque invisible devient une image claire.
Le silence de la chambre accompagne la pensée.
Comme une impression, l'image revient.
La mémoire de l'enfance transforme le présent.
Le lecteur observe la forme de la phrase.


  Show answer
1 memory transforms sensation. 2 reader rereads phrase. 3 image remains visible. 4 memory returns. 5 perception changes reading. 6 sensation becomes image. 7 silence accompanies thought. 8 image returns. 9 memory transforms present. 10 reader observes form.

Exercise Set 5 — Delay interpretation
For each sentence, write the order of operations: subject, verb, complement, attachment.

La mémoire transforme une sensation obscure en image.
Dans la chambre, une impression devient visible.
Le lecteur relit la phrase avec attention.
Sur la page, une distinction reste difficile.
Le temps transforme la perception du souvenir.


  Show answer
1 subject La mémoire; verb transforme; complement une sensation obscure; attachment en image. 2 attachment Dans la chambre; subject une impression; verb devient; complement visible. 3 subject Le lecteur; verb relit; complement la phrase; attachment avec attention. 4 attachment Sur la page; subject une distinction; verb reste; complement difficult state. 5 subject Le temps; verb transforme; complement la perception du souvenir.

Review Task — Skeleton before meaning
Choose three sentences from the mini reading. For each one, write:

opening frame if any;
subject;
conjugated verb;
complement if any;
one attachment.

Check Your Answer
You are succeeding if you can postpone interpretation. Do not ask first, “What does the whole thing mean?” Ask first, “Where is the subject, and where is the conjugated verb?”
What You Can Now Do
You can approach a French sentence as a structure. You can find the core before chasing every word. You can treat length as attachment, not magic.
Next Chapter
Chapter 006 remains paused until Chapters 001–005 have been practiced and reviewed. The next action is not expansion. It is to use these five chapters with real reading and self-testing.

Proustian/Question-Gradient.title: Question-Gradient
Proustian/Question-Gradient.content:
Question Gradient
Root Question
How does Proust train the reader to discover truth through signs, sensation, attention, misrecognition, and artistic form?
Starting Questions

What sign appears before it is understood?
What kind of sensation starts the reading process?
What kind of delay, mistake, or misrecognition organizes the scene?
What secondary lens clarifies the passage without replacing Proust?
What form of attention does the passage train?
How can this passage become a reader-facing card?

U1｜Signs / Method
How does Proust train the reader to read signs rather than merely follow plot, psychology, or memory?
Method entrance:

U1 General Introduction: From the Memory Cliché to Polycentric Reading

Supporting questions:

What forces thought before interpretation begins?
What makes a sign readable?
How does Deleuze help without replacing Proust?

U2｜Memory / Time / Space
How does Proust transform memory from recollection into a structure of signs, time, space, and artistic discovery?
Supporting questions:

How does the Madeleine scene turn sensation into discovery?
How does involuntary memory reopen time through place and sensation?
How does habit shape what can or cannot be perceived?

U3｜Music / Ineffable
How does Vinteuil’s music move from emotional sign to artistic truth, ineffable experience, and novelistic structure?
Supporting questions:

How does music carry truth before it can be explained?
How does the little phrase move from love sign to art sign?
What does the ineffable allow the novel to think?

U4｜Visuality / Gaze / Photography / Attention
How does Proust transform seeing into a discipline of attention, misrecognition, capture, and artistic truth?
Supporting questions:

How does the Vermeer yellow wall become a test of attention?
How does seeing differ from understanding?
How do gaze, framing, and capture organize misrecognition?

U5｜Space / Sensory History
How do spaces and sensory environments in Proust produce social time and historical subjectivity?
Supporting questions:

How do rooms and salons become social machines?
How do bells gather collective time?
How do smell and atmosphere mark social boundaries?

U6｜Writing Apparatus
How can U1–U5 be transformed into teachable, writable, reader-facing forms without losing aesthetic and intellectual force?
Supporting questions:

How does a Passage Card become a reader-facing block?
How does a Unit Digest become a course page?
How does the website remain a reading garden rather than a content dump?

Proustian/U1-General-Introduction-Memory.title: U1｜General Introduction: From the Memory Cliché to Polycentric Reading
Proustian/U1-General-Introduction-Memory.content:
U1｜General Introduction: From the Memory Cliché to Polycentric Reading
U1 is not a signs unit. It is the general introduction that uses the memory cliché as a methodological hinge: from involuntary memory to competing reading lenses, from single-center interpretation to claim/problem chains, and finally back to Proust’s textual world.
Position｜U1 as General Introduction
U1 establishes the course’s methodological tendency. It does not ask the reader to replace memory with signs, nor to choose Deleuze as the master key. It shows how the cliché “Proust is a novelist of memory” becomes the first pressure point from which the whole course opens.
Not This｜Signs as Course Center
U1 should not make “signs” into a new sovereign center. Deleuze remains useful, but he is only one theoretical line among several.
But This｜Memory Cliché as Methodological Hinge
The course begins with the force and insufficiency of involuntary memory, then unfolds multiple reading paths that return to the novel.

Core formulation: U1 is a methodological overture. It explains how Proustian 2.0 reads through strong theoretical positions without allowing any one of them to own Proust.

The Memory Cliché as Starting Pressure
The tradition of involuntary memory is not a weak opponent. It is powerful enough to become a recurring object of criticism, compression, displacement, and renewal. U1 must therefore begin by granting its force before showing why it cannot remain the only center.
English Claim
Memory is powerful but insufficient.
Proust is often entered through lost time, involuntary memory, and the return of the personal past. This entry is legitimate, but incomplete. If memory becomes the first and final explanation, the novel’s errors, delays, social codes, musical pressures, visual fragments, and artistic discoveries are flattened.
中文判断
记忆是强传统，但不是最终中心。
非自愿记忆当然构成《追忆》中最具震动性的经验之一。但如果它成为唯一解释，小说中的误读、延宕、社交姿态、爱情迷误、音乐压力、视觉凝聚与艺术真理都会被压成“过去回来了”。

U1 does not reject memory. It uses memory as the first hinge through which Proustian reading moves from a single strong tradition toward a polycentric method.

Basic Literature Review as Method
The literature review in U1 should not be a bibliography dump. It should present reading positions: what each lens sees, what it risks, and how it returns to the Proustian text-world.









































Reading PositionWhat It SeesWhat It RisksReturn to TextMemory TraditionLost time returns through sensation, involuntary memory, and the sudden recovery of personal history.Reducing the novel to recollection, nostalgia, or psychological recovery.Ask what returns, and why the return is delayed, unstable, or transformed.DeleuzeSigns force thought; the narrator learns through error, apprenticeship, and interpretation.Flattening prose into taxonomy or turning Proust into Deleuze.Ask whether signs clarify the passage, or whether classification weakens its literary pressure.PouletMemory becomes space; moments and places condense into fields of vision.Freezing narrative movement into static contemplation.Ask what spatial image or mosaic-like arrangement the passage forms.Narrative DiscourseMeaning emerges through delay, order, duration, frequency, voice, retrospection, and narrative arrangement.Over-formalizing the text and losing the pressure of experience.Ask how the passage becomes readable only through narrative structure.Visual / Music / Sensory PathsProust transforms image, sound, smell, gesture, and atmosphere into literary form.Drifting into art history, musicology, or sensory history without textual return.Ask how the medium is absorbed by the novel rather than simply added to it.
Polycentric Reading｜No Center Does Not Mean No Judgment
U1 introduces a polycentric method. “No center” does not mean arbitrary wandering. It means no single theory is allowed to become sovereign. Each lens must become strong enough to make a claim, produce a problem, and submit itself to textual testing.
Rule 1｜No single theory owns Proust.
Memory, signs, space, narrative delay, music, visuality, and sensory history are all possible entrances, not final masters.
Rule 2｜Every lens must become strong.
A weak lens produces decoration. A strong lens produces a claim, a problem, and a pressure against other readings.
Rule 3｜The text tests every claim.
A theory is useful only when it returns to a sentence, scene, rhythm, object, gesture, sound, or misrecognition.
Claim / Problem Chain
This is the central writing method for U1. The goal is not to list themes, but to unfold claims until their problems, counterclaims, limits, and textual returns become visible.








































StepActionFunction1ClaimState what a reading position asserts.2PassageAttach the claim to a concrete Proust scene.3ProblemShow what the claim cannot easily explain.4Counter-ClaimLet another lens answer or resist it.5LimitExpose where the second lens also begins to fail.6ReturnGo back to the prose and form a judgment.

Method principle: The more fully a claim/problem chain is unfolded, the more testable, comparable, and recoverable the reading becomes. This is U1’s version of rigor.

Kite-Line Reading｜Textual Spine and Theoretical Lines
The hand-drawn model becomes the course’s visual method: theory flies outward from the text, reaches its horizon, dissolves, and returns.
English Formulation
The text is the spine.
Theories are lines released above it. Each line may fly outward, rise, diverge, and open a new field of vision. But every line must return to the Proustian text-world.
中文表述
文本是脊骨。
理论是在文本脊骨上方放飞的线束。每条理论线都可以飞出、分叉、升高，但最终必须重新降落到普鲁斯特的句子、场景、感官与叙事运动之中。

Proustian 2.0 does not reject theory. It releases theory from the text, lets it fly to its horizon, watches it dissolve, and then returns to the novel and to the reader’s own perception.

Reading Action｜U1 Trains Method, Not Sign Classification
The reading action no longer begins by asking “what kind of sign is this?” It begins with the passage and asks what pressure appears. Signs are one possible lens, not the center.

Start with a Proust passage, not a theory.
Identify the dominant pressure: memory, error, delay, image, sound, social gesture, sensation, or artistic form.
Choose one provisional lens: memory, signs, space, narrative discourse, visuality, music, or sensory history.
Ask what this lens makes visible in the passage.
Ask what this lens fails to see, weakens, or over-systematizes.
Let another lens answer, resist, or intensify the first claim.
Return to the prose: sentence, rhythm, scene, gesture, object, sound, or image.
Produce a readerly judgment: what did this passage teach the reader to see?

Core Lenses Opened by U1
U1 introduces several strong reading lenses. Each one is provisional. Each one must return to the passage.
Memory

What lost past returns?
What sensory shock triggers it?
Why is return not enough?

Signs

What pressure forces interpretation?
What does the narrator misread?
Where does apprenticeship begin?

Space / Vision

What spatial image forms?
How do moments and places become a mosaic?
What does vision compress?

Narrative Discourse

What is delayed?
Who knows what, and when?
How does narrative order make meaning possible?

Music / Visuality

How does another art enter the novel?
Does the novel imitate it or transform it?
What new form of truth appears?

Sensory / Social Space

How do smell, sound, room, salon, or street produce social time?
What historical pressure enters private experience?

Scene Anchors as Test Cases
These are not proof examples for a single theory. They are testing grounds where multiple lenses compete and return.
Madeleine
Memory, sensation, sign, habit, delay, and narrative reorganization.
Swann / Odette
Love, jealousy, deception, interpretation, social signs, and misreading.
Names of Places
Fantasy, expectation, disappointment, space, language, and desire.
Vinteuil
Music, love, ineffable truth, repetition, and artistic transformation.
Vermeer
Visual attention, art sign, mortality, color, detail, and judgment.
Transition to U2–U6
U1 opens the whole course. It does not close itself around Deleuze or signs. Its output is a method that can move into later units.








































Question Opened in U1Later UnitCourse FunctionWhy is memory powerful but insufficient?U2｜Memory / Time / SpaceTurns recollection into structure, delay, space, and passage-level reading.How do signs, errors, and forced thought train the reader?U1 bridge + U2Provides a portable method without making Deleuze the center.How does music become a path toward truth?U3｜Music / IneffableMoves from emotional motif to artistic and novelistic structure.How does seeing become attention and judgment?U4｜Visuality / GazeReads visual fragments as pressures on perception and form.How do spaces and sensations produce social time?U5｜Sensory History / Social SpaceLinks private sensation with historical and social form.How can reading become a reader-facing structure?U6｜Writing ApparatusConverts U1–U5 into pages, cards, labs, and course architecture.
Final Judgment
The center is not memory, not signs, not Deleuze, not Poulet, and not any single theory. The center is the disciplined effort to approach Proust’s novel through competing, testable, returnable reading paths.
